headline: A Nobel for Anne Carson. She was listening to the wind.
summary: Canadian poet Anne Carson, 76, won the Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday. The Swedish Academy cited a "bold and inventive" body of work that plays with the Greek classics and makes new forms from them. She taught classics for over 30 years. The call found her in Iceland, "listening to the wind." It pays 12 million kronor, about $1.2m.

cover_question.q: How do you pick the best writer?

cover_answer: A committee in Sweden votes. This year it picked her.
table_question: Who gets to say which book is the best?

5-7.script: A poet in Canada named Anne Carson just won the biggest prize in the world for writing. A poet makes pictures out of words, and hers come from old Greek stories, older than the oldest castle. When the phone rang with the news she was in Iceland, listening to the wind. She was surprised and very happy.
5-7.why: A phone ringing in the wind is a scene a six-year-old can hold. The prize is the happy ending.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the phone ringing while she listens to the wind, and the Greek stories older than castles, and leaves the kronor out. Expect "what did she write?" Poems, and a book that is a poem and a story at once.

8-12.script: A committee in Sweden picks one writer a year for the Nobel Prize in Literature, the biggest prize in books. This year it is Anne Carson, a Canadian poet who taught ancient Greek for 30 years and writes poems that work like novels. Like science fair judges, they score the whole table, not one project.
8-12.why: Judges scoring the whole table is a mechanism they know from school.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults apply them fairly, so the script hands them the chain: a committee, a lifetime of books, one winner a year. The science fair judge is a mechanism they already own. Expect "is she the best writer in the world?" The committee says so this year. Last year it said a Hungarian novelist.

13-17.script: How do you pick the best writer? A committee in Sweden just gave Anne Carson the Nobel Prize in Literature for a lifetime of poetry, fiction and scholarship. Second: she taught ancient Greek for 30 years. Do her new forms need the old ones first?
13-17.why: Two true things: new forms, and 30 years in the old ones.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: she made new forms, and she spent 30 years inside the oldest ones. The script puts the committee's words next to her classics career and asks which came first. A prize for taste is safe ground to argue on. Expect "who decides what's good?" A committee in Sweden, this year. They could be wrong.

5-7.a: Someone who makes pictures out of words. Anne Carson's come from old Greek stories, and she just won the biggest prize for them.

8-12.a: The committee called her work "bold and inventive": new kinds of writing out of old Greek stories.
12 million kronor, about 1.2 million dollars, for a lifetime of books.

13-17.q: How do you pick the best writer?
13-17.a: A committee judges a lifetime of work, not one book. This year "bold and inventive" won.
Hers are novels in verse and essays in tangos. The Swedish Academy read them.
